lessons.title: Wave Behaviour
lessons.description: Transverse and longitudinal waves, wave speed, frequency, wavelength and amplitude.
lessons.content_html:
Types of Wave

Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. The particles of the medium vibrate about their rest positions but do not travel along with the wave. There are two main categories of wave:

• Transverse waves — the vibrations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. The wave forms crests (peaks) and troughs. Examples include light waves, water surface ripples, all electromagnetic waves, and waves on a string.
• Longitudinal waves — the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Instead of crests and troughs, longitudinal waves have compressions (particles pushed close together) and rarefactions (particles spread apart). Sound waves are the main example at GCSE.

An important distinction: mechanical waves (such as sound and water waves) require a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel through. Electromagnetic waves (such as light) do not need a medium and can travel through a vacuum.

Key Fact

Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Transverse: vibrations perpendicular to travel (crests and troughs). Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to travel (compressions and rarefactions).

Wave Properties

All waves — whether transverse or longitudinal — can be described using four key properties:

• Amplitude — the maximum displacement from the rest (equilibrium) position. Measured in metres. A larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy. For sound, greater amplitude means a louder sound; for light, it means brighter light.

• Wavelength (\(\lambda\)) — the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest, or compression to compression). Measured in metres.

• Frequency (\(f\)) — the number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). For sound, higher frequency means a higher pitch.

• Period (\(T\)) — the time for one complete wave to pass a point, measured in seconds. Period and frequency are reciprocals: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\). A wave with a frequency of 50 Hz has a period of \(\frac{1}{50} = 0.02 \text{ s}\).

The Wave Speed Equation

The relationship between wave speed, frequency and wavelength is:

$$v = f \times \lambda$$

Where \(v\) is wave speed (m/s), \(f\) is frequency (Hz), and \(\lambda\) is wavelength (m). This equation applies to all waves. You can rearrange it to find frequency (\(f = \frac{v}{\lambda}\)) or wavelength (\(\lambda = \frac{v}{f}\)).

Question: A sound wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Calculate the wave speed.

Answer: \(v = f \times \lambda = 500 \times 0.68 = 340 \text{ m/s}\). This is the speed of sound in air at room temperature.

Reflection, Refraction and Diffraction

Waves can interact with boundaries and obstacles in three important ways:

• Reflection — a wave bounces off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal — an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface). The wave speed, frequency and wavelength do not change during reflection.

• Refraction — a wave changes speed when it passes from one medium to another (e.g. from air into glass). If the wave hits the boundary at an angle, it also changes direction. The wave bends towards the normal when it slows down (entering a denser medium) and away from the normal when it speeds up (entering a less dense medium). The frequency stays the same but the wavelength changes.

• Diffraction — a wave spreads out when it passes through a gap or around the edge of an obstacle. The effect is greatest when the gap width is similar to the wavelength of the wave. If the gap is much larger than the wavelength, there is very little diffraction.

In a ripple tank, you can observe reflection, refraction and diffraction of water waves. A vibrating bar creates plane (straight) waves, and a lamp above projects the wave pattern onto a screen below. To measure wave speed: use a strobe light to “freeze” the waves, measure the distance between several wave crests and divide by the number of wavelengths to find \(\lambda\). Count the frequency from the motor speed. Then calculate \(v = f\lambda\).

For sound speed, you can use the echo method: stand a measured distance from a wall, clap and time how long the echo takes to return. The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is twice the distance to the wall. Speed = total distance ÷ time. To improve accuracy, time multiple echoes and divide.

Key Fact

Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Refraction: wave changes speed (and may change direction) at a boundary. Diffraction: wave spreads through gaps — most when gap width ≈ wavelength.

Sound waves have wavelengths of roughly 0.1 m to 10 m — similar in size to everyday gaps like doorways and corridors. This means sound diffracts significantly around corners, which is why you can hear someone in the next room even if you cannot see them. Visible light has an extremely short wavelength (about \(400\text{–}700 \text{ nm}\), or \(4 \times 10^{-7}\) to \(7 \times 10^{-7}\) m). Doorways are millions of times wider than light’s wavelength, so light shows almost no diffraction around everyday objects and travels in straight lines.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Wave equation questions are straightforward: write \(v = f\lambda\), substitute and solve. Make sure frequency is in Hz and wavelength in metres. For reflection and refraction diagrams, always draw and label the normal, incident ray, and reflected/refracted ray. State whether the wave speeds up or slows down to explain the direction of bending. For diffraction, state that the effect is greatest when the gap width is close to the wavelength.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Transverse waves: vibrations perpendicular to travel (light, water, EM waves). Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to travel (sound, with compressions and rarefactions).
  • Wave properties: amplitude, wavelength (\(\lambda\)), frequency (\(f\)), period (\(T = \frac{1}{f}\)). Wave speed: \(v = f\lambda\).
  • Reflection: angle in = angle out. Refraction: wave changes speed and may bend at a boundary. Diffraction: wave spreads through gaps (greatest when gap ≈ wavelength).

lessons.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.description: EM spectrum regions, uses, hazards, and how waves transfer energy.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Electromagnetic Waves?

Electromagnetic (EM) waves are transverse waves that can travel through a vacuum (empty space) — they do not need a medium. This is what makes them fundamentally different from mechanical waves like sound. In a vacuum, all EM waves travel at the same speed — the speed of light:

$$c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$$

EM waves are produced by changes in atoms and their nuclei, or by oscillating charges (such as electrons moving back and forth in an aerial). They transfer energy from a source to an absorber. Because the wave equation \(v = f\lambda\) still applies, and the speed is fixed in a vacuum, a higher frequency always means a shorter wavelength — and vice versa.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic spectrum is a continuous range of waves, ordered by wavelength and frequency. From longest wavelength (lowest frequency) to shortest wavelength (highest frequency):

Radio waves → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma rays

There are no sharp boundaries between the regions — the spectrum is continuous, and one type of wave blends gradually into the next. Our eyes can only detect the visible light portion, which ranges from red (longest visible wavelength, about 700 nm) to violet (shortest, about 400 nm). Everything else in the spectrum is invisible to us but can be detected with instruments.

Key Fact

All EM waves travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum. The spectrum ranges from radio (long wavelength, low frequency, low energy) to gamma (short wavelength, high frequency, high energy). Visible light is a small section in the middle.

• Radio waves (wavelength up to km): TV and radio broadcasts, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi. Can induce oscillations in electrical circuits, which is how aerials receive signals.

• Microwaves (wavelength cm): microwave ovens (water molecules absorb the energy), satellite communication, mobile phone networks.

• Infrared (IR) (wavelength μm): thermal imaging cameras, remote controls, heating (toasters, grills), fibre optic communications, night-vision goggles. All warm objects emit IR radiation.

• Visible light (400–700 nm): human vision, photography, fibre optic data transmission, laser surgery.

• Ultraviolet (UV): fluorescent lamps, security marking (invisible ink that glows under UV), sterilising water, detecting forged banknotes.

• X-rays: medical imaging of bones and teeth, airport security scanners, checking welds in pipelines.

• Gamma rays (shortest wavelength): cancer treatment (radiotherapy — targeted beams kill cancer cells), sterilising medical equipment and food, detecting leaks in pipes (industrial tracers).

Hazards of EM Radiation

Higher frequency EM waves carry more energy per photon and can therefore be more dangerous to living tissue. The key hazards are:

• Infrared: can cause skin burns if exposure is prolonged (e.g. sitting too close to a fire).
• Ultraviolet: causes sunburn, premature skin ageing, and increases the risk of skin cancer. Can also damage the eyes (leading to cataracts). Sunscreen and UV-blocking sunglasses reduce exposure.
• X-rays: can damage cells and DNA, potentially leading to cancer. Medical exposure is carefully controlled — lead aprons shield staff, exposure times are minimised, and the number of X-rays is limited.
• Gamma rays: the most penetrating and most energetic. Can cause cell mutation and cancer with prolonged exposure. In medical use, beams are tightly focused and the surrounding healthy tissue is shielded.

Key Fact

UV, X-rays and gamma rays can damage human tissue. Higher frequency = higher energy = more hazardous. The benefits of their use in medicine must be weighed against the risks.

Absorption, Transmission and Reflection

Different substances interact with EM waves in different ways, depending on the wavelength of the radiation and the nature of the material:

• Absorption: the wave's energy is taken in by the material and usually converted to heat. For example, dark surfaces absorb visible light, and your skin absorbs UV.
• Transmission: the wave passes through the material without being absorbed. For example, glass transmits visible light, and X-rays pass through soft tissue.
• Reflection: the wave bounces off the surface. For example, mirrors reflect visible light, and metal surfaces reflect radio waves.
• Refraction: the wave changes speed (and may change direction) when entering a different material. This is how lenses focus light.

A given material may absorb some wavelengths, transmit others, and reflect the rest. For example, glass transmits visible light but absorbs UV. The atmosphere transmits visible light and radio waves but absorbs most UV, X-rays and gamma rays — which is fortunate for life on Earth.

Radio waves have a unique property at GCSE level: they can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. When electrons oscillate (move back and forth) in a transmitter aerial at a certain frequency, they generate radio waves at that same frequency. Conversely, when radio waves reach a receiver aerial, they induce oscillations (an alternating current) in the aerial circuit. This is the basis of all radio communication — from AM/FM radio to Wi-Fi and mobile phones. The frequency of the oscillation must match the frequency of the wave for efficient transmission and reception.

Since all EM waves travel at \(c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\) in a vacuum, you can calculate the wavelength of any EM wave if you know its frequency, using \(\lambda = \frac{c}{f}\). For example, a radio station broadcasting at 100 MHz: \(\lambda = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{100 \times 10^6} = 3 \text{ m}\). An X-ray with frequency \(3 \times 10^{18}\) Hz: \(\lambda = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{3 \times 10^{18}} = 1 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}\) (about the size of an atom).
lessons.exam_tip_html: EM spectrum questions often ask you to compare wavelengths, frequencies and energies across the spectrum, or to give uses and hazards for specific regions. Be precise: say ‘X-rays are used for medical imaging to detect broken bones’ rather than just ‘hospitals’. For calculations, all EM waves travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum, so you can use \(v = f\lambda\) or \(\lambda = \frac{c}{f}\). Watch out for unit prefixes — MHz = \(\times 10^6\), nm = \(\times 10^{-9}\).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All EM waves are transverse, travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum, and do not need a medium. Spectrum: radio (longest \(\lambda\), lowest \(f\)) to gamma (shortest \(\lambda\), highest \(f\)).
  • Each region has specific uses. UV, X-rays and gamma rays can be hazardous to human tissue because higher frequency means more energy per photon.
  • Substances can absorb, transmit, reflect or refract EM waves depending on the wavelength and the material. Radio waves can be produced by and induce oscillations in electrical circuits.

lessons.title: Radioactivity
lessons.description: Isotopes, alpha, beta and gamma radiation, nuclear equations and half-life.
lessons.content_html:
Atomic Structure and Isotopes

Every atom has a nucleus made of protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons (negative charge) orbit the nucleus at different energy levels. The number of protons defines the element (its atomic number). In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. We write isotopes using nuclear notation: \(^A_Z X\) where \(A\) is the mass number (protons + neutrons) and \(Z\) is the atomic number (protons). For example, carbon-12 (\(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 (\(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

Key Fact

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Some isotopes have unstable nuclei that emit radiation — this is radioactive decay. The process is random and spontaneous.

Types of Radiation

Unstable nuclei can emit three main types of radiation (P7.1):

• Alpha (\(\alpha\)) particles — 2 protons + 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus, \(^4_2\text{He}\)). Strongly ionising because of their large charge and mass. Weakly penetrating: stopped by paper, skin or a few centimetres of air.
• Beta (\(\beta\)) particles — a high-speed electron emitted when a neutron converts into a proton. Moderately ionising and moderately penetrating. Stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
• Gamma (\(\gamma\)) rays — electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus. Weakly ionising but highly penetrating. Only significantly reduced by thick lead or several metres of concrete.

Alpha decay: the nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Mass number decreases by 4, atomic number decreases by 2. Example:

$$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$

Beta decay: a neutron converts to a proton, emitting a high-speed electron. Mass number stays the same, atomic number increases by 1. Example:

$$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$$

Gamma emission: the nucleus releases excess energy as a gamma ray. No change to mass number or atomic number. Gamma is often emitted alongside alpha or beta decay.

In all nuclear equations, the mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance on both sides.

Key Fact

Alpha: mass number −4, atomic number −2. Beta: mass number unchanged, atomic number +1. Gamma: no change to either. Mass and atomic numbers must balance in decay equations.

Ionisation

Ionisation occurs when radiation knocks electrons from atoms, creating ions. Alpha particles are the most ionising (because of their large charge and mass), followed by beta, then gamma. Ionisation in living cells can damage DNA, potentially causing mutations or cancer. The greater the ionising power, the more damage to cells — but higher ionising power also means lower penetrating power, because the radiation transfers its energy quickly.

The activity of a radioactive source is measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. In the laboratory, a Geiger-Müller (GM) tube connected to a counter measures the count rate (counts per second or per minute), which is proportional to the activity of the source.

When investigating radioactivity, you must account for background radiation. Take a background count (with no source present), then subtract it from all measurements. This corrected count rate represents radiation from the source alone. Radioactive decay is random, so repeating measurements and calculating averages improves reliability.

The nuclear model of the atom developed over time. Thomson proposed the ‘plum pudding’ model (positive charge spread throughout with embedded electrons). Rutherford’s gold foil experiment (1909) disproved this: most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, but some were deflected and a few bounced back. This showed the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. Bohr later refined the model with electrons in fixed energy levels (orbits) around the nucleus.

Half-Life

Half-life is the time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei (or the activity) of a sample to halve. Radioactive decay is random and unpredictable — we cannot predict when an individual nucleus will decay, but we can predict the average behaviour of a large number of nuclei (P7.1d).

After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives, a quarter remain. After three, an eighth. For example, if a sample has an activity of 800 Bq and its half-life is 3 hours, after 9 hours (3 half-lives): \(800 \rightarrow 400 \rightarrow 200 \rightarrow 100\) Bq.

The fraction of radioactive nuclei remaining after \(n\) half-lives can be calculated using the formula: $$\text{fraction remaining} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$ For example, after 5 half-lives the fraction remaining is \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5 = \frac{1}{32}\). If the original activity was 6400 Bq, the activity after 5 half-lives would be \(6400 \times \frac{1}{32} = 200\) Bq.

Key Fact

Half-life is the time for half the unstable nuclei to decay. Decay is random — you can’t predict individual atoms, only the average behaviour of many atoms.

Key Fact

After \(n\) half-lives, the fraction remaining is \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\). This formula lets you calculate the remaining activity or mass without repeated halving.

Background radiation is the low-level radiation that exists all around us. Natural sources include radon gas from rocks (the largest source in the UK), cosmic rays from space, and radioactive isotopes in food and building materials. Artificial sources include medical X-rays and the nuclear industry, but these contribute only a small fraction of total exposure.

When measuring the count rate of a radioactive source in the lab, you must subtract the background count rate first to get the corrected count rate. This ensures your measurement reflects only the source, not the environment.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For decay equation questions, check that mass numbers and atomic numbers balance on both sides. For half-life calculations, draw a table or use repeated halving — show every step. If given a graph, read off the time it takes for the count rate to halve from any starting point. Remember: alpha is most ionising but least penetrating; gamma is most penetrating but least ionising. Always subtract background radiation from experimental count rates.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons. Unstable isotopes decay, emitting alpha, beta or gamma radiation.
  • Alpha: most ionising, least penetrating (stopped by paper). Beta: moderate. Gamma: least ionising, most penetrating (reduced by lead).
  • Half-life = time for activity to halve. Decay is random. After \(n\) half-lives, fraction remaining = \(\frac{1}{2^n}\). Always subtract background radiation.

lessons.title: Uses and Dangers of Radiation
lessons.description: Penetration properties, contamination vs irradiation, and medical uses.
lessons.content_html:
Uses of Radioactive Materials

Radioactive materials have many practical uses in medicine, industry and research. The choice of which type of radiation to use depends on its penetrating power and ionising ability (P7.2a).

• Medical tracers: a patient swallows or is injected with a radioactive tracer (a gamma-emitting isotope with a short half-life, e.g. technetium-99m). Gamma rays pass through the body and are detected externally, allowing doctors to image organs and diagnose conditions such as cancer or kidney blockages.
• Radiotherapy: high doses of gamma rays or beta particles are targeted at cancerous tumours to kill the rapidly dividing cells. The beam is rotated around the patient so healthy tissue receives a lower dose while the tumour receives a concentrated dose.
• Sterilisation: gamma rays are used to sterilise medical equipment and food by killing bacteria. The food does not become radioactive.

Key Fact

Gamma emitters with short half-lives are used as medical tracers. Radiotherapy targets tumours with high-dose radiation. Gamma rays sterilise equipment and food without making them radioactive.

Industrial and Other Uses

• Thickness gauges: beta radiation is passed through materials like paper or aluminium foil during manufacturing. A detector on the other side measures how much gets through. If the material is too thick, the detector reading drops and the rollers adjust automatically.
• Smoke alarms: contain a small source of alpha radiation (americium-241). Alpha particles ionise air molecules, creating a small current. Smoke particles absorb the alpha radiation, reducing the current and triggering the alarm.
• Carbon dating: the proportion of carbon-14 (a radioactive isotope) in dead organic material decreases over time as it decays. By measuring the remaining carbon-14, scientists can estimate how old archaeological samples are (up to about 50,000 years).

The choice of radioactive isotope for a particular use depends on three properties: the type of radiation emitted, the half-life and the toxicity. For medical tracers, a gamma emitter with a short half-life (e.g. technetium-99m, half-life 6 hours) is ideal because gamma penetrates the body, and the short half-life means the patient is not exposed to radiation for long. For industrial thickness gauges, a beta emitter with a longer half-life is preferred so the source does not need frequent replacement.

In radiotherapy for cancer treatment, the radiation must be carefully targeted to maximise damage to the tumour while minimising harm to surrounding healthy tissue. Techniques include using multiple beams from different angles that converge on the tumour, so healthy tissue receives a low dose from each beam while the tumour receives a high combined dose.

Nuclear power stations use controlled nuclear fission (the splitting of heavy nuclei like uranium-235) to generate electricity. The process produces large amounts of energy from small amounts of fuel with no CO\(_2\) emissions during generation. However, it creates radioactive waste of varying levels of danger, and the risk of accidents (though rare) has significant consequences.

When selecting a radioactive source for any application, scientists weigh up the benefits (medical diagnosis, energy generation, industrial efficiency) against the risks (radiation exposure, contamination, waste disposal). This risk-benefit analysis is central to responsible use of radioactive materials. For OCR Gateway, you should be able to evaluate the benefits and risks of using radiation in given scenarios and justify whether the use is appropriate.

It is essential to distinguish between contamination and irradiation (P7.2b):

Contamination means a radioactive material is deposited on or inside the body. This is dangerous because the source continues to emit radiation in close contact with tissues. Contamination is removed by washing or decontamination procedures.

Irradiation means being exposed to radiation from an external source. The person does not become radioactive. The risk depends on the type and duration of exposure. Once the source is removed, the irradiation stops.

Contamination is generally considered more dangerous than irradiation because the radioactive material remains in contact with the body, giving continuous exposure that cannot be stopped simply by moving away.

Key Fact

Contamination = radioactive material on/in the body (ongoing risk). Irradiation = exposure to external radiation (stops when source is removed). Contamination is more dangerous because it provides continuous exposure.

Workers handling radioactive materials follow strict safety procedures (P7.2c):

• Minimise exposure time — spend as little time near sources as possible.
• Maximise distance — radiation intensity decreases with the square of the distance from the source.
• Use shielding — lead-lined containers, concrete walls and lead aprons absorb radiation.
• Wear protective equipment — gloves and lab coats prevent contamination.
• Monitor exposure — workers wear film badges or dosimeters that record their cumulative radiation dose.
• Use tongs — never handle radioactive sources directly; use long-handled tongs to increase distance.

Radioactive waste is classified by its activity and half-life. High-level waste (from nuclear reactors) must be stored securely for thousands of years, often in deep geological storage facilities. Low-level waste (contaminated clothing, gloves) is compacted and stored in shallow landfill sites.

Key Fact

Safety measures: minimise time, maximise distance, use shielding, wear protective equipment, monitor exposure with dosimeters, use tongs. High-level waste needs long-term secure storage.

Explain why that type is chosen: gamma for tracers because it penetrates the body; alpha for smoke alarms because it is strongly ionising but absorbed by smoke. For contamination vs irradiation, define both clearly and state which is more dangerous with a reason.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Radiation is used in medicine (tracers, radiotherapy), industry (thickness gauges, smoke alarms) and research (carbon dating).
  • Contamination (radioactive material on/in the body) is more dangerous than irradiation (external exposure) because it provides continuous exposure.
  • Safety precautions include minimising time, maximising distance, using shielding, wearing protection and monitoring exposure.

lessons.title: Work Done, Energy and Power
lessons.description: Conservation of energy, energy stores and transfers, work done and power.
lessons.content_html:
Conservation of Energy

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores. In any closed system, the total energy before a process equals the total energy after. Energy that seems to ‘disappear’ has been dissipated — spread out into less useful thermal energy in the surroundings (P6.1a).

Energy can be stored in different ways: kinetic (moving objects), gravitational potential (objects at height), elastic potential (stretched or compressed objects), chemical (food, fuels, batteries), thermal (hot objects), magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear. Energy transfers between these stores via heating, radiation, electrical current or mechanical work.

Key Fact

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It transfers between stores (kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, chemical, thermal, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear). Dissipated energy is wasted as heat.

Work Done

When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done. Work done is a measure of energy transferred. The equation is (P6.1b):

$$W = F \times d$$

where \(W\) = work done in joules (J), \(F\) = force in newtons (N), and \(d\) = distance moved in the direction of the force in metres (m). One joule of work is done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m.

Example: a person pushes a box with a force of 50 N across 3 m. Work done = \(50 \times 3 = 150\) J. This 150 J of energy has been transferred from the person’s chemical energy store to the kinetic energy store of the box (and some to thermal energy through friction).

When work is done against gravity (e.g. lifting an object), energy is transferred to the object’s gravitational potential energy store. The equation is:

$$GPE = m \times g \times h$$

where \(m\) = mass in kg, \(g\) = gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg on Earth) and \(h\) = height gained in metres. For example, lifting a 5 kg bag to a shelf 2 m high: \(GPE = 5 \times 9.8 \times 2 = 98\) J.

Similarly, a moving object has kinetic energy calculated by:

$$KE = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$$

where \(v\) = speed in m/s. Notice that kinetic energy depends on \(v^2\) — doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. This is why braking distance increases dramatically at higher speeds and why speed limits exist in residential areas.

Power measures how quickly energy is transferred (P6.1c). The equations are:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \quad \text{and} \quad P = \frac{W}{t}$$

where \(P\) = power in watts (W), \(E\) = energy transferred in joules (J), \(W\) = work done in joules (J), and \(t\) = time in seconds (s). One watt equals one joule per second.

Example: a 60 W light bulb transfers 60 J of energy every second. If it is on for 5 minutes (300 s), total energy transferred = \(60 \times 300 = 18{,}000\) J = 18 kJ.

A more powerful device transfers the same amount of energy in less time. This is why a 2000 W kettle boils water faster than a 1000 W kettle — it transfers energy at twice the rate.

Key Fact

Work done: \(W = F \times d\) (joules). Power: \(P = E/t\) or \(P = W/t\) (watts). Power measures the rate of energy transfer — higher power means faster energy transfer.

Efficiency

No energy transfer is 100% efficient. Some energy is always dissipated as waste heat. Efficiency measures how much of the input energy is usefully transferred (P6.1d):

$$\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$$

Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal (0 to 1) or as a percentage (multiply by 100). For example, a motor that receives 500 J of electrical energy and does 350 J of useful work has efficiency = \(\frac{350}{500} = 0.70\) = 70%. The remaining 150 J is dissipated as heat and sound.

Engineers design systems to minimise energy waste and improve efficiency:

• Lubrication — reduces friction between moving parts, decreasing the thermal energy wasted.
• Streamlining — reduces air resistance on vehicles, so less energy is wasted overcoming drag.
• Thermal insulation — slows heat transfer from buildings (loft insulation, double glazing, cavity wall insulation), keeping homes warmer with less heating.
• LED lighting — converts a higher proportion of electrical energy into light compared to incandescent bulbs, which waste most energy as heat.

Improving efficiency is important for reducing fuel consumption, lowering energy bills and decreasing carbon emissions from fossil fuels.

In calculations, you may need to combine the work, power and efficiency equations. For example, if a crane with 40% efficiency lifts a 2000 N load through 15 m in 30 seconds, the useful work done is \(2000 \times 15 = 30{,}000\) J. Since only 40% of the input energy is useful: total input energy = \(\frac{30{,}000}{0.4} = 75{,}000\) J. The power of the crane = \(\frac{75{,}000}{30} = 2{,}500\) W = 2.5 kW.

Elastic potential energy is stored when a spring or elastic material is stretched or compressed. The equation is:

$$EPE = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times e^2$$

where \(k\) = spring constant in N/m and \(e\) = extension in metres. Like kinetic energy, elastic potential energy depends on the square of the extension — doubling the stretch quadruples the energy stored. This equation applies only within the limit of proportionality, where force and extension are directly proportional (Hooke’s Law).

Key Fact

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. No device is 100% efficient. Wasted energy can be reduced through lubrication, streamlining, insulation and using more efficient technologies like LEDs.

Efficiency must be ≤ 1 (or ≤ 100%) — if your answer is higher, check your working.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is conserved: it transfers between stores but is never created or destroyed. Dissipated energy is wasted as heat.
  • Work done = force × distance (\(W = Fd\)). Power = energy ÷ time (\(P = E/t\)). Both are measured in standard SI units.
  • Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. Reduce waste through lubrication, insulation and efficient technologies.

lessons.title: Energy Resources and Sustainability
lessons.description: Renewable and non-renewable energy sources, efficiency and sustainability.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Resources

The main energy sources available on Earth fall into two categories:

• Non-renewable sources — will eventually run out. These include fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and nuclear fuel (uranium, plutonium). Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms. They are being consumed far faster than they can form.
• Renewable sources — are replenished naturally and will not run out. These include solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, wave and biomass (P6.2a).

Key Fact

Non-renewable sources (fossil fuels, nuclear) will run out. Renewable sources (solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, wave, biomass) are replenished naturally. Nuclear is non-renewable but does not produce CO\(_2\) during generation.

Environmental Impacts

Every energy resource has environmental consequences (P6.2b):

Fossil fuels release CO\(_2\) when burned, contributing to the greenhouse effect and climate change. They also release sulfur dioxide (causing acid rain) and particulates (causing respiratory problems). Oil spills damage marine ecosystems.
Nuclear power produces no CO\(_2\) during generation and is very reliable, but creates radioactive waste that remains dangerous for thousands of years and must be stored securely. There is also risk of nuclear accidents (e.g. Chernobyl, Fukushima).

Renewable sources generally produce little or no CO\(_2\) during operation, making them crucial for tackling climate change. However, they often have significant land use requirements (solar farms, wind farms) and can affect local ecosystems and communities. The embodied energy in manufacturing solar panels and wind turbines must also be considered, though this is typically repaid within a few years of operation.

The carbon footprint of an energy source considers the total greenhouse gas emissions across its entire lifecycle — from construction through operation to decommissioning. On this measure, wind, solar, nuclear and hydroelectric all have much lower footprints than fossil fuels. Natural gas has the lowest carbon footprint of the fossil fuels (about half that of coal per unit of energy), which is why it is sometimes called a ‘transition fuel’ as countries move towards renewables.

Energy demand varies throughout the day (peak demand in the evening) and throughout the year (higher in winter). Baseload power stations (nuclear, gas) run continuously to meet minimum demand, while renewable sources and gas turbines provide additional capacity during peaks. The growing use of battery storage and pumped hydro storage helps balance intermittent renewable supply with variable demand.

Solar: no pollution during operation, low running costs. Disadvantages: expensive to install, dependent on sunlight (ineffective at night or in cloudy weather), large areas needed for solar farms.

Wind: no pollution during operation, free fuel. Disadvantages: intermittent (only generates when wind blows), visual and noise impact, can harm birds.

Hydroelectric: reliable, can respond quickly to demand, no fuel costs. Disadvantages: requires damming rivers, which floods valleys, displaces communities and destroys habitats.

Tidal: very predictable (tides are regular), no pollution. Disadvantages: very expensive to build, limited suitable locations, can affect marine ecosystems.

Geothermal: reliable, low emissions, small land footprint. Disadvantages: only available where hot rocks are near the surface (volcanic regions), high drilling costs.

Biomass: carbon-neutral in theory (CO\(_2\) absorbed during growth equals CO\(_2\) released during burning). Disadvantages: requires land to grow fuel crops (competing with food production), still produces pollutants when burned.

Key Fact

Renewable sources produce little or no CO\(_2\) during operation but many are intermittent or require specific locations. No energy source is perfect — each has trade-offs between cost, reliability and environmental impact.

The National Grid

The National Grid is a network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to consumers across the country (P6.2c). Electricity is transmitted at high voltage and low current through overhead power lines. This is because energy loss due to heating in the cables is proportional to the current squared (\(P = I^2 R\)). Using high voltage reduces the current and therefore reduces energy wasted as heat in the cables.

Step-up transformers at power stations increase the voltage (to 400,000 V) for efficient long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers near homes reduce the voltage (to 230 V) for safe domestic use.

The UK is transitioning from fossil fuels to renewables to reduce carbon emissions and improve energy security (not relying on imported fuels). The energy mix — the combination of sources used — is changing: wind and solar capacity is increasing while coal use has virtually ended.

Challenges include the intermittency of wind and solar (requiring backup from gas or nuclear), the need for energy storage (e.g. batteries, pumped hydro storage) and the cost of upgrading infrastructure. Nuclear power is being considered as a reliable low-carbon baseload source to complement renewables.

Key Fact

The National Grid transmits electricity at high voltage (low current) to reduce energy losses (\(P = I^2 R\)). Step-up transformers increase voltage for transmission; step-down transformers reduce it for safe domestic use.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Non-renewable sources (fossil fuels, nuclear) will run out; renewables (solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass) are replenished naturally.
  • Fossil fuels cause climate change (CO\(_2\)), acid rain (SO\(_2\)) and pollution. Nuclear is low-carbon but produces radioactive waste.
  • The National Grid transmits at high voltage/low current to minimise heating losses. Step-up and step-down transformers control voltage.

lessons.title: Physics on the Move
lessons.description: Stopping distances, braking forces, momentum conservation in safety features.
lessons.content_html:
Speed, Distance and Time

The OCR Gateway specification requires you to know typical speeds for everyday scenarios: walking (~1.5 m/s), running (~3 m/s), cycling (~6 m/s), cars in town (~13 m/s or 30 mph), motorway driving (~30 m/s or 70 mph), speed of sound in air (~340 m/s), and wind speeds which vary widely (P8.1a).

Speed is the distance travelled per unit time. The equation is:

$$\text{speed} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} \quad \text{or} \quad v = \frac{s}{t}$$

where \(v\) = speed in m/s, \(s\) = distance in metres, \(t\) = time in seconds. Speed can also be measured in km/h for longer journeys.

Key Fact

Speed = distance ÷ time (\(v = s/t\)). Typical speeds: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, car on motorway 30 m/s, sound in air 340 m/s.

Velocity and Acceleration

Velocity is speed in a given direction. It is a vector quantity (has both magnitude and direction), while speed is a scalar (magnitude only). An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction is constantly changing.

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (P8.1b):

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

where \(a\) = acceleration in m/s\(^2\), \(v\) = final velocity, \(u\) = initial velocity, \(t\) = time. Positive acceleration means speeding up; negative acceleration (deceleration) means slowing down.

Example: a car accelerates from rest (\(u = 0\)) to 20 m/s in 8 seconds. Acceleration = \(\frac{20 - 0}{8} = 2.5\) m/s\(^2\). If the same car then brakes from 20 m/s to rest in 4 seconds, the deceleration = \(\frac{0 - 20}{4} = -5\) m/s\(^2\). The negative sign indicates slowing down.

An object in free fall near the Earth’s surface accelerates at approximately \(9.8\) m/s\(^2\) (often rounded to \(10\) m/s\(^2\) for calculations). This is the acceleration due to gravity, denoted \(g\). In the absence of air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of their mass — a key insight from Galileo’s experiments.

The relationship between force, mass and acceleration (Newton’s Second Law) can also be written as \(a = \frac{F}{m}\), showing that for a given force, a heavier object accelerates less. This explains why a fully loaded lorry takes much longer to stop than an empty car travelling at the same speed — both the greater mass and the greater kinetic energy (\(KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\)) increase the braking distance.

Distance-time graphs show how far an object has travelled over time (P8.1c). A straight line means constant speed; a steeper gradient means faster speed. A horizontal line means the object is stationary. A curve means the speed is changing (accelerating or decelerating). The gradient of the line equals the speed.

Velocity-time graphs show how velocity changes over time. A horizontal line means constant velocity. A positive gradient means acceleration; a negative gradient means deceleration. The area under the line equals the distance travelled. A steeper gradient means greater acceleration.

To calculate the area under a velocity-time graph for irregular shapes, split it into rectangles and triangles. Area of a triangle = \(\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}\).

Key Fact

Distance-time graphs: gradient = speed. Velocity-time graphs: gradient = acceleration, area under graph = distance. Straight lines = constant speed or constant acceleration.

Reaction Time and Stopping Distance

Reaction time is the delay between seeing a hazard and responding. Typical human reaction time is 0.2–0.9 seconds. Factors that increase reaction time include tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions and age.

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance (P8.1d). Thinking distance is the distance travelled during the driver’s reaction time. Braking distance is the distance travelled once the brakes are applied. Factors increasing braking distance include wet or icy roads, worn tyres, worn brakes and higher speed. At higher speeds, the braking force needed is greater, which means more energy must be transferred to heat in the brakes.

Newton’s First Law: an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays at constant velocity, unless acted on by a resultant (unbalanced) force.
Newton’s Second Law: \(F = m \times a\) — the resultant force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. A larger force produces a larger acceleration; a larger mass reduces the acceleration for the same force.
Newton’s Third Law: for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force. These act on different objects.

When an object falls, it initially accelerates due to gravity. As speed increases, air resistance increases until it equals the gravitational force. At this point, the resultant force is zero and the object reaches terminal velocity — falling at a constant speed.

Key Fact

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Newton’s Second Law: \(F = ma\). At terminal velocity, air resistance equals weight and acceleration is zero.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For graph interpretation questions, always identify what the gradient and area represent before answering. For distance-time: gradient = speed. For velocity-time: gradient = acceleration, area = distance. Show all calculation working with units. For stopping distance questions, always state both thinking distance and braking distance separately, then add them. Name specific factors for each.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Speed = distance/time. Velocity = speed + direction. Acceleration = change in velocity/time (\(a = (v-u)/t\)).
  • Distance-time graphs: gradient = speed. Velocity-time graphs: gradient = acceleration, area = distance travelled.
  • Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Newton’s Second Law: \(F = ma\).

lessons.title: Global Challenges in Physics
lessons.description: The Solar System and Beyond, satellite orbits, gravitational attraction, and the life cycle of stars.
lessons.content_html:
The Solar System and Beyond

Our solar system consists of the Sun (a star), eight planets, dwarf planets (such as Pluto), moons, asteroids and comets. The four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and rocky. The four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are much larger gas or ice giants (P8.3a).

The solar system is part of the Milky Way galaxy, which contains billions of stars. The universe contains billions of galaxies, each with billions of stars. Distances in space are so vast that we measure them in light-years — the distance light travels in one year (about \(9.46 \times 10^{12}\) km).

Key Fact

The solar system has eight planets: four rocky inner planets and four gas/ice outer giants. It sits within the Milky Way galaxy. Distances are measured in light-years.

Satellite Orbits

Satellites orbit planets due to gravitational attraction. Artificial satellites are placed in two main types of orbit (P8.3b):

• Geostationary orbit — the satellite orbits once every 24 hours, staying above the same point on Earth. Used for communications (TV, phone) and weather monitoring. These orbits are high (~36,000 km above Earth) and positioned above the equator.
• Polar orbit (low Earth orbit) — the satellite passes over both poles, orbiting much closer to Earth (~200–2000 km). As the Earth rotates beneath it, the satellite can scan the entire surface over time. Used for mapping, military surveillance and environmental monitoring.

Humans have explored space using telescopes (ground-based and space-based like the Hubble and James Webb), robotic probes (e.g. Mars rovers like Perseverance), and crewed missions (e.g. the International Space Station). Space exploration has provided valuable knowledge: understanding the origins of the universe, discovering exoplanets, and developing technologies with everyday applications (satellite navigation, weather forecasting, water purification) (P8.3c).

Challenges of space exploration include the extreme distances involved (even light takes ~4 years to reach the nearest star), the hostile environment (radiation, vacuum, microgravity effects on the body), and the enormous cost. Despite these challenges, international collaboration (e.g. NASA, ESA) continues to push the boundaries of exploration.

Gravity is the force responsible for keeping planets in orbit around the Sun, and moons in orbit around planets. The gravitational force depends on the masses of the two objects and the distance between them. Closer objects and more massive objects experience stronger gravitational attraction. This is why the inner planets orbit faster than the outer planets — they are closer to the Sun’s gravitational pull.

The orbital speed of a satellite depends on its altitude. Lower orbits require higher speeds (the ISS orbits at ~7.7 km/s). Higher orbits require lower speeds (geostationary satellites orbit at ~3 km/s). If a satellite’s speed is too low for its orbit, it will spiral inward; too high and it will move to a higher orbit or escape entirely.

Key Fact

Geostationary satellites orbit once per 24 hours above the equator (for communications). Polar orbit satellites are lower and scan the whole Earth (for mapping and monitoring).

The Life Cycle of Stars

Stars form from nebulae — clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls the material together, and as it compresses, it heats up. When the core is hot enough, nuclear fusion begins (hydrogen fuses into helium), and a star is born. The star enters its main sequence phase, where it remains stable for billions of years as the outward pressure from fusion balances the inward pull of gravity (P8.3d).

When a star runs out of hydrogen fuel, its fate depends on its mass:

• Sun-sized stars: expand into a red giant, then shed outer layers to form a planetary nebula, leaving behind a white dwarf which gradually cools.
• Massive stars: expand into a red supergiant, then explode in a supernova. The core collapses to form either a neutron star or, if massive enough, a black hole. Supernovae scatter heavy elements into space, which form new stars and planets.

The Big Bang theory states that the universe began from an extremely hot, dense point approximately 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since. Evidence for this includes:

• Red shift — light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum. This shows galaxies are moving away from us. The further away a galaxy, the greater its red shift, meaning it is moving away faster.
• Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) — low-level microwave radiation detected from all directions in space. This is the remnant heat from the Big Bang, predicted by the theory and discovered in 1965.

These observations support the conclusion that the universe is expanding. Scientists continue to study dark matter and dark energy, which appear to make up most of the universe but remain poorly understood.

Key Fact

Stars form from nebulae. Sun-sized stars become red giants, then white dwarfs. Massive stars go supernova, forming neutron stars or black holes. Red shift and CMBR are evidence for the Big Bang and expanding universe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For OCR Gateway questions on the life cycle of stars, describe the stages in order for both sun-sized and massive stars. Use correct terminology (main sequence, red giant/supergiant, supernova). For red shift, explain what it tells us about how galaxies are moving. A common mistake is confusing red shift with Doppler shift in sound — while the principle is similar, in the exam refer specifically to light from galaxies.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The solar system has eight planets; the Milky Way has billions of stars; the universe has billions of galaxies.
  • Geostationary orbits (high, 24-hour period) are for communications; polar orbits (low, scanning) are for mapping and monitoring.
  • Stars form from nebulae and end as white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes. Red shift and CMBR are evidence for the Big Bang.
